content: The absorptive state refers to the physiological period during which the gastrointestinal tract is actively digesting and absorbing nutrients, and anabolic processes (building up of molecules) surpass catabolic processes (breaking down of molecules). During this state, glucose serves as the primary energy source. Carbohydrate Processing: Simple sugars absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract are transported to the liver, where they are converted into glucose. This glucose is either released into the bloodstream for immediate use by body cells or stored as glycogen and triglycerides. Glycogen is stored in the liver, while triglycerides are stored in adipose tissue as energy reserves for later use during the post-absorptive state. Any remaining glucose is taken up by body cells for energy or stored in skeletal muscle as glycogen. Triglyceride Processing: Triglycerides, the primary products of fat digestion, are packaged into chylomicrons. These chylomicrons are broken down into fatty acids and glycerol by the enzyme lipoprotein lipase, allowing them to pass through capillary walls. Most of these fatty acids and glycerol are reassembled into triglycerides and stored in adipose tissue. A smaller portion is utilized for energy production in adipose cells, skeletal muscle, and hepatocytes (liver cells). In conditions of low carbohydrate availability, other body cells may also begin to use triglycerides as an energy source. Amino Acid Processing: Amino acids absorbed from dietary protein are processed in the liver. The liver deaminates (removes the amino group from) amino acids, converting them into keto acids, which can then enter the Krebs cycle to produce ATP. Some amino acids are converted into fat stores, while others are used to synthesize plasma proteins. However, the majority of amino acids exit the liver through the sinusoids and are taken up by body cells to construct proteins necessary for cellular function and repair.
